subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 11 periods = 440 minutes
Total: 11 periods · 7h 20min

periods.textbook_anchor: Here Comes the Rain! — Write at least two clues for why it will or will not rain today (p. 87)

time_bands.activity: The teacher invites children to step outside briefly or look out of the window and silently study the sky — cloud cover, colour, wind direction, humidity on skin. Back inside, the teacher asks: 'What did you notice? What did the sky tell you?' Children share freely.

Children open Textbook p. 87 and complete the 'Write' task — noting at least two clues that suggest rain is coming and at least two that suggest it is not. The teacher prompts: 'What do elders in your home notice before it rains? What do animals or plants do?' encouraging local and elder knowledge alongside direct observation.

Pairs share their clues with each other, then a few children read their clues to the class. The teacher lists the clues on the board under two columns — 'Rain likely' and 'Rain unlikely' — and invites children to spot any clues that appear in both, sparking a brief discussion on uncertainty in prediction.

Children write one final sentence in their notebooks: 'The sky clue I find most reliable is … because …' They underline the clue and keep the notebook open for quick sharing. The teacher closes by affirming that careful observation is how both scientists and farmers read the sky.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify observable environmental clues and use them to make a reasoned prediction.
periods.section_context: Sky observation clues (cloud cover, wind, humidity, animal behaviour, elder knowledge), rain prediction task with at least two clues for each side.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Has an elder ever told you a sure sign of rain — something in the sky, on the ground, or with animals?' Draw out traditional indicators naturally; do not label or separate them from children's own clues.

periods.activity_title: Watching Rain Fall — Observing and Drawing
periods.textbook_anchor: Here Comes the Rain! — Draw a picture of the rain that you observed (p. 88)
materials: A vessel (bowl or cup) to collect rainwater if raining

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads aloud the rain-observation questions from Textbook p. 88 — heavy or light, drops big or small, fast or slow, straight or slanting, sheets of water, direction change. Children close their eyes and recall the last rain they witnessed, trying to picture each detail. They share brief oral descriptions.

Children open Textbook p. 88 and begin drawing their observed rain scene. The teacher encourages them to capture what makes their rain unique — slant of drops, size, any background detail like a tree bending or a puddle forming. If possible, a vessel is placed at the window to collect any current rain or children recall collected rainwater from a previous experience and note whether it looked clean or dirty beside their drawing.

Children add a caption to their drawing answering at least two of the textbook's observation questions — e.g. 'The rain was heavy. The drops were small and fell in sheets.' The class then does a quick gallery walk, moving between desks to see each other's drawings. Children notice differences in how classmates saw the same rain.

The teacher asks: 'Did everyone draw exactly the same rain? What does that tell us about observation?' Children share one-sentence responses. The teacher affirms that different observers notice different things, and that drawing helps us remember what we saw.

periods.implied_lo: Students can represent sensory observations of a natural event through drawing with descriptive annotation.
periods.section_context: Rainfall observation questions (intensity, drop size, speed, direction, sheets of water), collected rainwater appearance (clean or dirty), drawn rain scene with caption.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Encourage children who have never seen heavy rain to draw what they imagine or have heard described — their drawing is valid. Prompt: 'What would you hear? What would you feel on your skin?'

periods.textbook_anchor: What happened to the rainwater? — Did it rain only in your area or in other nearby places as well? Make a guess, then ask and find out (p. 89)
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram showing rain falling on different surfaces (soil, road, rock, pond)

time_bands.activity: The teacher draws a simple sketch on the board — rain falling on a patch of soil, a road, a rock, and a pond. The teacher asks: 'After the rain stops, what happens to the water in each place?' Children call out ideas freely; the teacher notes key words (soaks, flows, evaporates, collects) beside each surface.

Children open Textbook p. 89 and read (or the teacher reads aloud) the section on the journey of rainwater — soil absorption, groundwater, wells, streams, rivers, puddles, ponds and lakes. The teacher pauses after each destination and asks: 'Has anyone seen this happen near your home or village?' Children connect the text to local experience.

Small groups discuss the task from Textbook p. 89 — 'Did it rain only in your area or in other nearby places too? Make a guess, then find out.' Groups share their reasoning: How could they find out? Who might they ask? The teacher extends this to: 'How does water from the hills reach rivers far away?' connecting the local to a broader water journey.

Each child writes two sentences in their notebook: one naming a local water body (stream, pond, well, river, lake) and one guessing where the water in it came from. Children who know folk songs about rivers or rain share a line or two, enriching the session's closing.

periods.implied_lo: Students can trace the movement of rainwater across different surfaces and connect it to familiar local water bodies.
periods.section_context: Rainwater journey (soil absorption, groundwater, wells, streams, rivers, puddles, ponds, lakes), rain spread across nearby areas, local water body names.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Is there a river, pond or well near your village or neighbourhood? Does anyone know a story or song about it?' Let children name and describe local water bodies in their own language before introducing textbook vocabulary.

periods.textbook_anchor: What happened to the rainwater? — Find some songs about the rain or make up one, in your language or any other. Sing some songs about the rain (p. 89)

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: 'Does rain make everyone happy? Think of someone for whom rain might cause worry or difficulty.' Children discuss farmers waiting for rain, workers caught in a downpour, children playing in puddles, and people whose homes might flood. The teacher affirms all perspectives and notes them on the board.

Children open Textbook p. 89 and take up the rain-song task. The teacher invites children who already know a rain song — in any language — to hum or sing a line. Then, in small groups, children compose a short rain song or rhyme (three to five lines) in their home language, choosing one feeling about rain to express — joy, relief, worry, wonder.

Groups take turns performing their song or rhyme. The class listens for the feeling and the rain detail embedded in each piece. The teacher notes on the board the variety of feelings and languages represented, celebrating diversity of response to the same natural event.

Each child writes their group's song in their notebook and adds one sentence: 'Our song shows the feeling of … because …' The teacher closes by connecting expression to observation: what we feel about rain is shaped by what we see and what people around us need.

periods.implied_lo: Students can express observations of a natural event through a creative form that reflects a chosen perspective or feeling.
periods.section_context: Rain songs in multiple languages, feelings about rain (joy, relief, worry, wonder), different people's relationship to rainfall (farmers, workers, children, people at risk of flooding).
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Does your family sing or say anything special when rain comes? Is there a word in your language for the smell of rain on dry earth?' Let folk and regional expressions enter naturally without labelling them.

periods.activity_title: Where Does Our Tap Water Come From?
periods.textbook_anchor: Water is a Precious Gift! — Where do you get water from? Do you get water from a tap? If yes, ask the elders in your home from where the water comes into the tap (p. 91)
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram showing tap → pipe → rooftop tank → municipal supply → well / borewell / tanker / river

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens with: 'When you turn on a tap, where does that water come from?' Children respond freely. The teacher sketches a simple chain on the board as children contribute ideas — tap, pipe, tank, treatment plant, river, borewell — without correcting or leading yet.

Children open Textbook p. 91 and read (or listen to) the story of Surya and Barkha tracing their tap water. The teacher asks: 'Is your water journey the same as theirs? What is different?' Children share their home's water source — municipal tap, well, borewell, tanker, river, or someone who carries it. The teacher updates the board diagram with the children's local additions.

The class discusses the tasks from Textbook p. 91 — who carries water, how far, by what means. The teacher asks: 'Is there someone in your family or neighbourhood who carries water every day? What is that like?' Children are encouraged to speak with respect and gratitude about those who do this work.

Children write two sentences in their notebooks: 'Water comes to my home from … ' and 'Someone who helps bring water to our home or neighbourhood is … Thank you!' The teacher invites a few children to read their sentences aloud, reinforcing appreciation for people who make water accessible.

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe the human-made pathway that brings water from a source to their home and identify who keeps that pathway working.
periods.section_context: Tap water source tracing (rooftop tank, pipes, municipal supply, well, borewell, water tanker), people who carry or deliver water, Surya and Barkha's water journey.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Does anyone in the class know of a village where people walk a long way to fetch water? How do they carry it?' This brings water scarcity into the discussion without making any child feel singled out.

periods.activity_title: Water Storage Vessels — Then and Now
periods.textbook_anchor: Water is a Precious Gift! — Ask your grandparents or any elder: How did they get water? Did they use water in the same way as you do? How did they store water? Write a short story about what you found out (p. 93)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook page showing clay pot, clay surahi, copper vessel, brass pot, steel pot, aluminium pot, glass bottle, plastic bottle, plastic bucket

time_bands.activity: The teacher holds up or names several water storage containers — clay pot, steel pot, plastic bottle, glass bottle — and asks: 'Which of these do you have at home? Which do you think is oldest?' Children guess and share. The teacher introduces the idea that different materials keep water differently — cool, warm, clean — and that people chose vessels wisely.

Children open Textbook p. 93 and look at the range of vessels shown. The teacher reads the elder-interview task from the page. In pairs, children role-play the task: one child is the 'grandparent' and recalls (or invents based on what they know) the vessels used long ago and how water was stored before taps were common; the other child is the interviewer. They switch roles. The teacher circulates and prompts: 'What did the clay pot feel like? Why did people prefer it in summer?'

Children draw one vessel they find interesting — from the textbook or from their family — and write its name in their home language alongside the drawing. They note one reason people used or still use that vessel. The teacher asks the class: 'Why do you think clay pots were so popular before plastic arrived? What do they do that plastic cannot?'

Children write three to four sentences as a short story from the point of view of the elder they imagined — 'When I was young, we stored water in a … because …' A few children share their stories. The teacher affirms the variety of vessels and practices across regions of India.

periods.implied_lo: Students can connect changes in household practices over time by gathering and presenting information from elder knowledge.
periods.section_context: Water storage vessels (clay pot, clay surahi, copper vessel, brass pot, steel pot, aluminium pot, glass bottle, plastic bottle, plastic bucket), elder knowledge about past water-storage practices, role-play elder interview.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Does your grandmother or any elder still use a clay pot or surahi? Why? What does the clay do to the water?' This draws out material knowledge naturally and honours traditional practices without naming them as a special category.

periods.activity_title: How Much Water Do We Really Use?
periods.textbook_anchor: Water in Our Daily Lives — List all the activities you can think of for which we need water (p. 92)
materials: A mug or small container (if available)

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: 'From the moment you woke up this morning until you arrived here, how many times did you use water?' Children count silently on their fingers and then call out activities. The teacher writes them rapidly on the board in a running list — drinking, brushing teeth, washing face, bathing, cooking, flushing, mopping.

Children open Textbook p. 92 and complete the 'Write' task — listing all activities that need water. They compare their personal list with what is in the textbook and add any activities they had missed. The teacher then asks the estimation question from the same page: 'How many mugs of water do you need to brush your teeth? How much for a shower?' Children write their estimates.

The class discusses the estimates. The teacher (or a child) holds up a mug or traces its size in the air and asks: 'Is one mug enough to brush teeth? Three mugs? Ten?' Children debate and settle on a class estimate for each activity. The teacher lists the activity-and-estimate pairs on the board and asks: 'Which activity uses the most water? Does that surprise you?'

Children write their final list with estimates in their notebooks — at least five activities with the number of mugs or buckets estimated for each. They circle the activity that uses the most water. The teacher closes with: 'Tomorrow, try to actually count. See if your estimate was right.'

periods.implied_lo: Students can list and estimate the quantity of water consumed across daily activities and identify which uses the most.
periods.section_context: Daily water-use activities (drinking, brushing teeth, bathing, cooking, washing, flushing), mug-count estimation for brushing teeth and showering.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Does everyone use the same amount of water for the same activity? What might make the amount different — family size, region, season?' Prompt children to think beyond their own household.

periods.activity_title: Vessels Exhibition — Drawing and Displaying Water Containers
periods.textbook_anchor: Water in Our Daily Lives — On a separate sheet of paper draw a picture of any vessel that you find interesting and write its name in your language. Put up an exhibition of these pictures in your classroom (p. 94)
materials: Tape or pins to display drawings on wall or board
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 94 vessel images for reference

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens Textbook p. 94 and reads aloud the exhibition activity instructions. Children look at the vessel illustrations in the textbook. The teacher invites quick sharing: 'Has anyone used or seen any of these at home or at a relative's home? Which one do you want to draw?' Children choose their vessel.

Children draw their chosen water vessel on a separate sheet of paper and write its name in their home language (and in English or the medium of instruction if they know it). They add any patterns, decorations, or distinctive features they remember or observe in the textbook. The teacher circulates, asking: 'Why did you choose this vessel? What do you like about it?'

Children tape or pin their drawings on the classroom wall or board, creating a class exhibition. The teacher leads a gallery walk — children move around quietly observing each other's drawings. The teacher prompts: 'How many different kinds of vessels can you count? Do any have patterns or decorations? Can you see which materials were most common?'

The class reconvenes and shares observations from the gallery walk. Children note in their notebooks: how many different vessels are displayed and whether they found patterns on any of them. The teacher affirms that this variety of vessels reflects the creativity and knowledge of people across India.

periods.implied_lo: Students can document and display observations of everyday objects through labelled drawing and interpret a collection of peer drawings for patterns.
periods.section_context: Water storage vessel identification and drawing (clay pot, clay surahi, copper vessel, brass pot, steel pot, aluminium pot, glass bottle, plastic bottle, plastic bucket), naming in home language, classroom exhibition, gallery walk for patterns.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Did anyone find a vessel that is decorated with patterns? Where do you think those patterns come from — a region, a craft tradition?' Let children speculate freely; this draws out awareness of craft without labelling it formally.

periods.activity_title: Building a Birdbath — Water for Birds
periods.textbook_anchor: Every Drop Counts — Prepare a birdbath: take a shallow and wide container, keep some stones for birds to perch, add fresh water, and keep in your yard, balcony or terrace (p. 97)
materials: A shallow wide container (old bowl, base of an old pot, or wide tray — one per group)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens with: 'In very hot weather, where do birds find water to drink?' Children discuss. The teacher asks: 'What would happen if there were no ponds, puddles, or streams nearby in summer?' This grounds the need for the birdbath in the birds' actual survival requirement.

Children open Textbook p. 97 and read the birdbath activity instructions together. Working in small groups, children assemble their birdbath using the available materials — shallow container, stones placed inside for perching, fresh water added. The teacher guides: 'How deep should the water be? Why not too deep? Where in school or at home could you place this so birds feel safe?'

Groups place their birdbaths in accessible spots (window ledge, corridor, courtyard) or plan where they would set one up at home. Each group decides on a maintenance plan — how often to change the water, how to clean it. Children record the plan in their notebooks: container used, stones placed, water depth, planned location, cleaning schedule.

The class discusses: 'Is giving water to birds a new idea or something people have done for a long time?' The teacher connects the practice to the broader tradition of keeping water for others — people and animals — especially in summer. Children write one sentence in their notebook: 'I will support birds by …'

periods.implied_lo: Students can plan and assemble a simple setup that addresses the water needs of another living being, and describe a maintenance routine for it.
periods.section_context: Birdbath construction (shallow wide container, stones for perching, fresh water, depth less than 10 cm), placement at home or school, maintenance plan (water change frequency, scrubbing twice a week), water needs of birds in summer.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Has anyone seen a clay or stone water trough left outside for animals or travellers? Is that still done in your neighbourhood?' This draws out the tradition of communal water-sharing without labelling it as a separate category.

periods.activity_title: Reflecting on Rain and Local Water — Writing and Drawing
periods.textbook_anchor: Every Drop Counts — Draw a picture of your birdbath. Write the names of the birds and insects that come to drink water from your birdbath (p. 98)

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads aloud the 'Let us reflect — Write' prompts from Textbook p. 98 — writing about rain observations and about a local water body. Children spend a moment recalling the rain they observed and any local stream, pond, well, or river they know, before picking up a pencil.

Children work independently on the two writing tasks from Textbook p. 98: a few lines on their rain observations (intensity, direction, cleanliness of collected water) and a few lines on a local water body (its name, whether its water is used for drinking, how it is carried home, and whether it was used in the past). The teacher circulates, prompting: 'What did the collected rainwater look like? Is the water body still used today or not?'

Children take up the 'Let us reflect — Draw' task from Textbook p. 98 — drawing their birdbath and writing beside it the names of any birds or insects they have seen or hope to see visiting it. Children who have not yet set up a birdbath draw the one their group assembled and name birds common in their area.

A few children share their drawings and a sentence from their writing. The teacher affirms the variety of local water bodies and birds across the class, reinforcing that water connects every living thing — from clouds to wells to birdbaths — in a continuous, precious flow.

periods.implied_lo: Students can present observations and inquiry findings about a natural resource through combined written and drawn expression.
periods.section_context: Rain observation writing (intensity, direction, cleanliness of collected rainwater), local water body writing (name, drinking use, transport, historical use), birdbath drawing with bird and insect names.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'What is the name of the water body near your village or neighbourhood in your language? Is there a story or legend connected to it?' Let local names and stories enter the reflection naturally.

periods.activity_title: Every Drop Counts — Pollution, Waste, and Solutions
periods.textbook_anchor: Every Drop Counts — Discuss among yourselves and list the activities due to which water gets polluted or wasted. Think of three solutions with your group and write them in your notebook (p. 99)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens Textbook p. 99 and reads the 'Let us reflect — Discuss' prompt aloud. The teacher then poses the anchor question to the class: 'What are the ways in which water in your home or neighbourhood gets wasted or made dirty?' Children call out freely; the teacher notes responses on the board in two columns — 'Wasted' and 'Polluted'.

Small groups take the discussion deeper — each group picks two items from the board (one waste, one pollution) and talks about why it happens and who is affected. Groups then brainstorm three concrete solutions they themselves could act on, not just suggest for others. The teacher circulates and prompts: 'Is this a solution you can actually do at home or school, or is it something only adults can do?'

Each group shares their three solutions with the class. The teacher writes the solutions on the board and asks the class to vote (thumbs up) for solutions that feel genuinely doable by a child. The teacher highlights the value of small, daily acts — like closing a tap — as real conservation, linking to the Indian tradition of treating water as sacred and sharing it with all living beings.

Each child writes their personal pledge in their notebook: 'I will help protect water by … (three actions).' Children read their pledges in pairs and encourage each other. The teacher closes by affirming that every drop saved by every child adds up to something real and meaningful.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify causes of water waste and pollution in their immediate environment and propose actionable conservation practices.
periods.section_context: Water pollution and waste causes (home and neighbourhood activities), three group-generated conservation solutions, personal water-conservation pledge, sacred and shared nature of water, water pots for passersby tradition.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Has anyone seen water pots kept outside a home or a temple for anyone passing by to drink? Why do people do that?' This draws out the water-sharing tradition as part of the discussion on conservation values.

assessment_items.question_text: Riya wants to know if it will rain today. Which of these is the BEST clue she should use?

options.label: A
options.text: Her friend told her it rained in a city very far away last week.

options.label: B
options.text: She woke up early and had a good breakfast this morning.

options.label: C
options.text: The classroom lights are switched on today.

options.label: D
options.text: The sky has thick, dark clouds and the air feels heavy and damp.

assessment_items.annotation: Accept any response that names a directly observable sky or environment clue — cloud colour, humidity, wind, animal behaviour. The key is that the clue must be observable by the child.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify observable environmental clues and use them to make a reasoned prediction.

competency.competency_text: Asks questions and makes predictions about simple patterns (season change, food chain, phases of the moon, movement of stars and planets, shapes of trees, plants, leaves, and flowers, rituals, celebrations) observed in the immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.B: Child has not connected rain prediction to environmental observation; they are naming personal events unrelated to weather.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Child confuses distant rain events with local prediction; they have not grasped the near-environment observation principle.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Child is listing any morning event rather than a weather clue; they have not identified what to look for in the environment.

assessment_items.question_text: Look at the picture of rain you drew. Write two things you noticed about the rain — for example, the size of the drops, whether it fell straight or at an angle, and whether the water you collected looked clean or dirty. Use your own words.
expected_elements: Names at least one physical feature of the rain observed (e.g. drop size, direction, intensity, sheets of water).
States whether the collected rainwater looked clean or dirty, with any observation about its appearance.
Uses sensory or descriptive language rather than a single-word answer.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept descriptions in the child's home language or mother tongue alongside English. Drawings labelled in vernacular are valid evidence. Regional variation in rain character (heavy monsoon, light drizzle, mountain rain) is expected and correct.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can represent sensory observations of a natural event through drawing with descriptive annotation.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

expected_elements: Names at least one physical feature of the rain observed (e.g. drop size, direction, intensity, sheets of water).
States whether the collected rainwater looked clean or dirty, with any observation about its appearance.
Uses sensory or descriptive language rather than a single-word answer.

assessment_items.question_text: After heavy rain, Arjun saw a big puddle in the road, a stream flowing behind his house, and the well in his courtyard was fuller than before. What does this show about rainwater?

options.label: A
options.text: Rainwater disappears into the air immediately after it falls.

options.label: B
options.text: Rainwater goes directly into the sea without passing through any other water body.

options.label: C
options.text: Rainwater moves to different places — it collects in puddles, flows into streams, and soaks into the ground to fill wells.

options.label: D
options.text: Rainwater only stays on the ground where it fell and never moves.

assessment_items.annotation: The correct response requires connecting multiple local observations (puddle, stream, well) to the concept of rainwater movement across surfaces and underground. A child who names only one destination has partial understanding.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can trace the movement of rainwater across different surfaces and connect it to familiar local water bodies.

competency.competency_text: Observes and identifies the natural (insects, plants, birds, animals, geographical features, sun and moon, stars, planets, natural resources) and social (houses, relationships) components in their immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.A: Child holds a misconception that rainwater evaporates instantly; they have not connected rainfall to visible water bodies.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Child has not grasped that water flows and is absorbed; they think water stays fixed in one spot.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Child has a partial understanding — water does eventually reach the sea — but misses the intermediate journey through local water bodies and groundwater.

assessment_items.task: Write and perform a short rain song or rhyme (three to five lines) in any language. Your song should show one feeling that rain brings — for example, joy, relief, worry, or wonder. Include at least one thing you have actually observed about rain.
assessment_items.scaffold: My rain song is about the feeling of ________. One thing I observed about rain is ________. My song: (write your lines here).
format_of_output: Written song or rhyme of three to five lines
One sentence naming the feeling expressed
Performance (singing or recitation) for the class or a partner
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any language including home languages and mixed-language compositions. Songs that reflect regional rain experiences (heavy monsoon, sparse desert rain, hill rain) are all valid. A child who writes fewer than three lines but includes a clear observation and feeling has met the core intent.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can express observations of a natural event through a creative form that reflects a chosen perspective or feeling.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The child can move from direct observation of a natural event to an expressive creative form that communicates both what they saw and how it felt.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold prompts the child to name the feeling first and ground the song in at least one observation. A child who fills both blanks and writes even three simple lines has met the task.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: song names a specific observable rain feature (slanting drops, smell, sound, puddles) and communicates a clear feeling; the two are connected. Weak: generic lines about rain with no observable detail and no identifiable feeling.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Children who have not experienced heavy rain can write about light drizzle, imagined rain, or rain they have heard described. Performance can be humming, whispering, or speaking — not only loud singing.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Creative written composition with oral performance
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: Matches the dominant mode C&E and the competency demand to present findings through creative modes including poem, play, and oral expression.

assessment_items.question_text: Priya gets water from a tap at home. Trace the journey of that water — name at least two steps the water passes through before it reaches her tap.
expected_elements: Names at least two steps in the water supply chain (e.g. river/lake/borewell → treatment/pump → rooftop tank → pipe → tap, or well → tanker → overhead tank → pipe → tap).
Shows that water passes through a human-made system before reaching the tap.
Uses at least one correct term for a part of the supply system (tank, pipe, borewell, tanker, pump).
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any locally accurate water supply chain — municipal, tanker-fed, borewell-fed, or river-fed systems are all correct. Regional variation in water supply systems is expected; do not penalise for naming a system different from the textbook example.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe the human-made pathway that brings water from a source to their home and identify who keeps that pathway working.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

expected_elements: Names at least two steps in the water supply chain (e.g. river/lake/borewell → treatment/pump → rooftop tank → pipe → tap, or well → tanker → overhead tank → pipe → tap).
Shows that water passes through a human-made system before reaching the tap.
Uses at least one correct term for a part of the supply system (tank, pipe, borewell, tanker, pump).

assessment_items.question_text: You asked an elder how they stored water when they were young. Name one vessel they used and explain one reason why people chose that vessel.
expected_elements: Names a specific vessel (e.g. clay pot, clay surahi, copper vessel, brass pot) that represents a past storage practice.
Gives a reason for choosing that vessel that is connected to a practical benefit (e.g. clay keeps water cool, copper keeps it clean, brass is durable).
The response reflects something learned from an elder or from the range of vessels discussed in class.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any vessel from the chapter's range or any vessel named by an elder at home — regional names in any language are valid. The reason does not need to use scientific vocabulary; 'it keeps water cold' is fully acceptable for Grade III. This item invites region-specific answers; accept any vessel and reason that reflects genuine elder knowledge.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can connect changes in household practices over time by gathering and presenting information from elder knowledge.

competency.competency_text: Connects changes in the environment and the lives of their family and community, as communicated by elders and through local stories (changes in occupation, food habits, resources, celebrations, communication)

expected_elements: Names a specific vessel (e.g. clay pot, clay surahi, copper vessel, brass pot) that represents a past storage practice.
Gives a reason for choosing that vessel that is connected to a practical benefit (e.g. clay keeps water cool, copper keeps it clean, brass is durable).
The response reflects something learned from an elder or from the range of vessels discussed in class.

assessment_items.question_text: Meena listed her morning water activities and estimated how much water she used. Which activity is MOST LIKELY to use the most water?

options.label: B
options.text: Rinsing her mouth once after brushing her teeth.

options.label: C
options.text: Taking a full bucket bath or shower.

options.label: D
options.text: Wiping her hands with a damp cloth.

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer reflects the estimation task from the section. A child who selects A or D may not have completed the mug-counting activity and has not developed a sense of relative water quantity.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can list and estimate the quantity of water consumed across daily activities and identify which uses the most.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

what_each_option_reveals.B: Child has not developed a sense of relative water quantity; they are not distinguishing between a large and small water use.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Child has picked the smallest water use without applying the estimation reasoning from the activity.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Child is associating water use with drinking alone and has not considered the full range of daily activities estimated in the task.

assessment_items.task: Draw one water storage vessel that you find interesting — it can be one you have at home, one an elder described to you, or one from the pictures in your textbook. Write its name in your language. Add one detail to your drawing — a pattern, a handle, a spout, or a material marking — that makes the vessel recognisable.
assessment_items.scaffold: The vessel I chose is called ________ in my language. I chose it because ________. (Draw the vessel here and add one detail.)
format_of_output: Labelled drawing of one vessel on paper
Name of the vessel in the child's language
One sentence giving a reason for choosing it
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any vessel from the textbook range or any vessel named by the child's family. Names in any regional language are valid and should be celebrated. Drawings do not need to be artistically detailed — a recognisable shape with one distinguishing detail meets the standard. This item invites region-specific answers; vessels and names that differ from the textbook list are correct.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can document and display observations of everyday objects through labelled drawing and interpret a collection of peer drawings for patterns.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The child can select, draw, and label an object from observation or memory, adding a distinguishing detail that shows they looked carefully.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold asks for a name and a reason — a child who provides both and draws a recognisable vessel with one detail has met the task fully.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: vessel is recognisable, labelled by name in any language, has a specific distinguishing detail (pattern, spout, material), and the reason reflects a genuine property (keeps water cool, easy to carry). Weak: unlabelled blob-like shape with no detail and no reason.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Children who do not know vessel names from their family can use textbook pictures as their reference. Children with difficulty drawing can describe the vessel in words alongside a rough sketch.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: Matches the dominant mode C&E and the exhibition task that required labelled vessel drawings, assessing the same skill in a retrievable format.

assessment_items.question_text: You built a birdbath for birds to use in summer. Name two things you did to make sure the birdbath was safe and useful for birds, and explain why each step matters.
expected_elements: Names at least two steps from the birdbath construction or maintenance (e.g. used a shallow container, placed stones for perching, kept water depth less than 10 cm, changed water regularly, cleaned with a scrubber).
For each step, gives a reason connected to the bird's need (e.g. shallow water so small birds do not drown, stones so birds can stand, fresh water so it is safe to drink).
Shows understanding that the birdbath requires ongoing care, not just a one-time setup.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any two steps from the activity and any reason that connects the step to the bird's wellbeing. Children who name the maintenance steps (changing water, cleaning) alongside construction steps show stronger understanding of sustained stewardship.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can plan and assemble a simple setup that addresses the water needs of another living being, and describe a maintenance routine for it.

competency.competency_text: Identifies needs of plants, birds, and animals, and how they can be supported (water, soil, food, care)

expected_elements: Names at least two steps from the birdbath construction or maintenance (e.g. used a shallow container, placed stones for perching, kept water depth less than 10 cm, changed water regularly, cleaned with a scrubber).
For each step, gives a reason connected to the bird's need (e.g. shallow water so small birds do not drown, stones so birds can stand, fresh water so it is safe to drink).
Shows understanding that the birdbath requires ongoing care, not just a one-time setup.

assessment_items.question_text: Write two things you observed about the rain and one thing you found out about a stream, river, well, pond, or lake near where you live. Use your own words.
expected_elements: Names two distinct observed features of rain (e.g. intensity, direction, drop size, whether collected water looked clean or dirty).
Names a local water body and includes at least one piece of information about it (its name, whether it is used for drinking, how water is carried from it, or whether it was used in the past).
Uses descriptive language that reflects direct observation or inquiry rather than copied definitions.
assessment_items.annotation: This item invites region-specific answers — local water body names, states of use, and rain character vary greatly across India. Accept any locally accurate response. Names of water bodies in regional languages are valid and correct.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can present observations and inquiry findings about a natural resource through combined written and drawn expression.

Names a local water body and includes at least one piece of information about it (its name, whether it is used for drinking, how water is carried from it, or whether it was used in the past).

assessment_items.question_text: Your group listed ways that water gets wasted or polluted in your home or neighbourhood. Choose one cause of water waste or pollution. Explain why it happens and suggest two actions that a child your age could actually do to help solve it.
look_for: Clearly names one specific cause of water waste or pollution drawn from the child's immediate environment (not a generic textbook phrase).
Explains why this cause happens — connecting it to a habit, a situation, or a need — rather than simply restating that water is wasted.
Proposes two actions that are genuinely within a child's capacity (e.g. closing a tap after use, telling a family member, using a mug instead of a running tap), not adult-only interventions.
The response shows that the child recognises water as a shared resource that everyone — including children — has responsibility for.
assessment_items.annotation: This item invites region-specific answers — causes of waste and pollution differ by household type, region, and season. Accept any cause and solutions that are locally accurate and child-actionable. A child in a water-scarce region may name different causes than a child in a water-abundant one; both are correct.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify causes of water waste and pollution in their immediate environment and propose actionable conservation practices.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates how natural resources can be shared, maintained, and conserved (trees, use of rainwater, benefits of millets)
